Short Communication Intrahepatic plasma cells, but not atypical memory B cells, associate with clinical phases of chronic hepatitis B

1 Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Erasmus University Medical Center, Rotterdam, the Netherlands 2 Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES), Department of Chemistry, and Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA 3 The Ragon Institute of Massachusetts General Hospital, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA 4 Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA 5 Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA 6 Department of Immunology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA 7 Liver Center, Division of Gastroenterology and Liver Center, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA 8 Clinical Translational Science Infectious Diseases, Janssen Research and Development, Beerse, Belgium 9 Toronto Centre for Liver Disease, Toronto General Hospital Research InstituteUniversity Health Network, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 10 Department of Immunology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 11 Department of Immunology, Erasmus University Medical Center, Rotterdam, the Netherlands

Studies have traditionally focused on the role of T cells in chronic hepatitis B (CHB), but recent evidence supports a role for B cells. The enrichment of so-called atypical memory (AtM) B cells, which show reduced signaling and impaired differentiation, is believed to be a characteristic feature of CHB, potentially contributing to the observed dysfunctional anti-HBsAg B-cell responses. Our study, involving 62 CHB patients across clinical phases, identified AtM B cells expressing IFNLR1 and interferon-stimulated genes. Contrary to previous reports, we found relatively low frequencies of AtM B cells in the liver, comparable to peripheral blood. However, liver plasma cell frequencies were significantly higher, particularly during phases with elevated viral loads and liver enzyme levels. Liver plasma cells exhibited signs of active proliferation, especially in the immune active phase. Our findings suggest a potential role for plasma cells, alongside potential implications and consequences of local proliferation, within the livers of CHB patients. While the significance of AtM B cells remains uncertain, further investigation is warranted to determine their responsiveness to interferons and their role in CHB.

## Introduction

For decades, immunological studies have focused on the role of T cells in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. However, emerging evidence has highlighted B cells in the immunopathogenesis of chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Dysfunctional anti-HBsAg B-cell responses, pronounced inﬁltration of B cells into the liver, and the enrichment of atypical memory (AtM) B cells are considered key features of CHB [1–3]. AtM B cells have been reported at increased frequencies in conditions of chronic antigen stimulation, such as HIV-1 infection, with reported frequencies ranging from 14–56% of the total circulating B-cell population [1, 4]. AtM B cells in CHB patients have attenuated B-cell receptor signaling, reduced capacity to secrete proinﬂammatory cytokines, and more importantly, impaired differentiation into antibody-secreting cells [5]. Compared with circulating classical memory B cells, AtM B cells express higher levels of T-Bet (TBX21), CD11c (ITGAX), and the inhibitory receptors FCRL5, PD-1, and BTLA in CHB patients, as determined by ﬂow cytometry [5]. As in HIV-1 infection, recent studies have reported an increased frequency of AtM B cells in CHB patients ranging from 4–17% of total circulating B cells, compared with 2–8% AtM B cells generally reported in healthy control individuals [1]. Although the relative frequencies of circulating AtM B cells are substantially lower in CHB compared with HIV-1 infection, it is speculated that the overall enrichment of AtM B cells may partly explain the defective anti-HBsAg antibody responses observed in CHB patients [5, 6]. Moreover, Burton et al. [5] reported that AtM B cells were found to be enriched in

the HBV-infected liver where viral replication occurs and where B cells have been found to accumulate around portal and periportal areas [3, 5]. To better understand the role and compartmentalization of AtM B cells in CHB, we performed single-cell RNA-sequencing on paired peripheral blood and liver ﬁne-needle aspirates (FNA) of CHB patients.

## Results and discussion

A total of 62 patients with CHB were included and classi- ﬁed into distinct clinical phases: immune tolerant (IT), immune active (IA), inactive carrier (IC), HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (ENEG), HBsAg-negative individuals (SNEG), and patients receiving nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUC) treatment (Table 1). We identiﬁed and annotated ﬁve B-cell clusters in blood and liver (Fig. 1A, Suppl. Table 1–3), including an AtM B-cell cluster identiﬁed by the expression of FCRL5 (fold change, FC: 4.8), ITGAX (FC: 2.8), TBX21 (FC: 2.3), and lower CXCR5 expression (FC: −1.6) when compared with classical memory B cells (Fig. 1B and C), in line with a previous publication [5]. In both blood and liver, AtM B cells highly expressed IFNLR1 (FC: 1.8) and interferon-stimulated genes such as MX1 (FC: 1.6), MX2 (FC: 1.3), OAS1 (FC: 1.5), and IFI30 (FC: 2.6) (Fig. 1C), suggesting responsiveness upon exposure to interferon. Moreover, in both blood and liver, AtM B cells showed low or undetectable gene expression levels of PDCD1 (PD- 1), CD274 (PD-1L), BTLA, and the liver-homing chemokine receptor CXCR3 (data not shown). found that AtM B cells were observed in relatively low frequencies within the liver comparable to frequencies observed in peripheral blood (median interquartile range [IQR]: 4.8% [7] and 3.5% [6] of total B cells, respectively; Fig. 1D). It is important to point out that Burton et al. [5] deﬁned atypical memory B cells by ﬂow cytometry, and that this deﬁnition may not be identical to our classiﬁcation of atypical memory B cells purely based on transcriptional signature. In addition, AtM B-cell frequencies in blood and liver did not ﬂuctuate between clinical phases of CHB (Fig. 1E), and relative frequencies remained low in each patient group generally representing less than 10% of total B cells. In contrast to the AtM B cells, we show signiﬁcantly higher plasma cell frequencies in the liver as compared with peripheral blood (median [IQR]: 10.8 [17] and 3.2% [7] of total B cells, respectively; P < .0001, Fig. 1D). Activated B cells can differentiate into antibody-producing plasma cells in germinal centers, typically providing long-lasting humoral protection. Liver plasma cell cluster frequencies ﬂuctuated throughout the CHB natural history (Fig. 1F) and were signiﬁcantly associated with clinical phases characterized by elevated viral loads and serum alanine transaminase levels (IA and ENEG). Interestingly, signs of active cell proliferation with a signiﬁcantly higher expression of MKI67 (FC: 4.5) were only detected in the liver plasma cell cluster (Table 3), predominantly observed in the IA phase of CHB (Fig. 1G, arrow). This was further conﬁrmed by cell cycle scoring analysis showing that 42% of 323 liver plasma cells in the IA phase are in the G2/M cell cycle phase (Fig. 1H). The additional cell cycle scoring analysis provides complementary information regarding the proliferative activity of cells beyond MKI67 expression alone and allows us to determine whether cells are indeed in the active phases of proliferation. We have previously shown that the total number of B cells in the liver is increased in the IA phase of CHB compared with healthy controls [3]. Our results suggest that the relative increase of B cells and plasma cells within the liver may be partly due to the local proliferation of plasma cells.

## Conclusion

Although more subtle interferon-mediated effects cannot be excluded, our data do not support a role for AtM B cells in CHB and question their signiﬁcance. Further research is needed to determine whether AtM B cells are functionally responsive to interferons [7], given the higher gene expression levels of interferon-stimulated genes and IFNLR1, and whether they are more responsive than other B-cell subsets. Our data indicates that plasma cells may play a role, alongside potential implications and consequences of local proliferation, within the livers of CHB patients. Although experimental evidence is lacking, it has been speculated by others that a functional cure of CHB may

occur through T-cell-mediated hepatocyte killing and antibodydependent cellular cytotoxicity, in which the anti-HBs antibody subclass and afﬁnity could contribute to a more effective localized immune response leading to functional cure [8]. Therefore, unraveling the role of plasma cells in CHB will be important to get more insights into humoral responses and this may guide novel therapeutic strategies aimed at inducing an effective immune response against HBV.

## Data limitations and perspectives

Our study utilized liver ﬁne-needle aspirates for single-cell sequencing of B cells, while others such as Zhang et al. [9] and Bai et al. [10] performed single-cell sequencing on core liver biopsies after enzymatic digestion of liver tissues and sorting of CD45-positive leukocytes. As reported previously, the use of liver ﬁne-needle aspirates avoids the time and sample manipulation involved with digestion and cell sorting and allows the collection of liver material from patients on a voluntary basis even without a medical indication to do so [11]. However, despite efforts to validate our ﬁndings using publically available datasets, the methodological differences prevented reliable comparisons between datasets. Our study focused on single-cell transcriptome sequencing of total B cells to provide a broader understanding of the global B-cell subsets in the blood and liver of chronic hepatitis B patients across different clinical phases. Since the absolute number of B cells in the liver is low, and the number of HBV-speciﬁc B cells even lower, we were unable to examine the HBV-speciﬁc Bcell transcriptome across the clinical phases in the current study. For similar reasons, additional subclustering of plasma cells and more functional studies to determine their characteristics could not be conducted in the current experimental setting. Future studies with a larger number of especially patients in the IA or ENEG clinical phase are needed to assess these features, which should also include B-cell receptor sequencing to assess B-cell receptor diversity and clonality.

## Material and methods

Study population

A cross-sectional cohort with a total of 62 chronic hepatitis B patients was included in this study. USA). The cohort included 5 IT, 4 IA, 18 IC, 4 ENEG, 20 SNEG, and 11 patients receiving NUC treatment (Table 1). All patients had no or minimal liver ﬁbrosis at the time of inclusion as determined by elastography (<7.0 kPa).

Collection of blood and liver fine-needle aspirates and sample preparation for single-cell RNA-sequencing

The collection of blood and liver samples and subsequent sample preparation was performed as described previously [11]. All samples were sequenced using the Seq-Well S3 platform. Seq-Well S3

libraries were pre-processed using the DropSeq pipeline with the tools v2.3.0 as previously described [12].

Analysis of scRNAseq data

Low-quality cells or empty droplets were ﬁltered by removing cells with <300 features and >20% of reads mapped to the mitochondrial genome. Cell doublets or multiplets were removed by excluding cells with >6000 features. For the regular single-cell analysis, the default settings from the Seurat pipeline in R were used for log normalization (scale.factor = 10 000), highly variable gene selection (method = “vst”, nfeatures = 5000), dimensionality reduction, and clustering (Louvain, resolution = 0.3, UMAP dims = 20, n.neighbors = 15). MS4A1+ CD79A/B+ B cells from both blood (8912 cells) and FNA (12 057 cells) were selected and re-clustered using the Louvain algorithm (resolution = 0.2) and clusters were visualized by UMAP (dims = 1:20, n.neighbors = 15). Cell clusters were annotated manually based on well-known lineage-speciﬁc markers retrieved from differentially expressed genes using the FindAllMarkers function (min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.6, only.pos = TRUE), including genes that were expressed in at least 10% of cells and with a signiﬁ- cant absolute fold change of 1.5 (P-adjusted < .05). P-values were obtained using the Wilcoxon rank sum test and adjusted using the Bonferroni correction method. Cell-cycle scores were calculated using the CellCycleScoring function in Seurat with default settings. Cells were classiﬁed in either G2/M, S, or G1 phase based on the expression of n = 54 G2/M phase and n = 43 S phase gene markers (Seurat cc.genes). R (version 4.2.2) and Graph- Pad Prism (version 8) were used for statistical analyses. Continuous variables were expressed as median with IQR. The Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test was used to determine signiﬁcant differences between B-cell cluster frequencies in blood vs. liver, and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied to assess signiﬁcant differences in relative frequencies of B-cell clusters in blood and liver between clinical phases of chronic hepatitis B (P < .05).
